passage: "Jaya, when I was about your age, I planted two bean seeds. One in the sun, one in the dark cupboard. I was sure the dark one would grow faster, because I thought seeds like to hide. I watered both every day. After a week, both sprouted! But the cupboard one was tall, thin and yellow, and the sunny one was short, strong and green. I was so surprised. That's when I learned to guess, then test, then look properly." Manoj pointed at her science book. "What's your guess about the ice cubes?"

qa.q: Where did Manoj plant the two bean seeds?
qa.a: One in the sun and one in the dark cupboard.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel about the dark-seed guess before and after the test?
qa.a: Manoj felt sure the dark seed would grow faster, thinking seeds like to hide, and was then surprised when the sunny one grew short, strong and green.

qa.q: What could Jaya learn from Manoj's story for her ice experiment?
qa.a: She could make a guess, test it and then look carefully at what actually happens.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel hearing that Manoj's guess was partly wrong?
qa.a: She might feel it's okay to guess wrong, since that's part of learning.

grounding: An elder tells a story of making a prediction, testing it and noticing the real result.

passage: Science class started in fifteen minutes, and Madhav and Zainab had forgotten their float-or-sink project. Zainab grabbed a bucket from the school canteen. They only had a spoon, an apple, a pencil and a lemon. "Guess first," Madhav said. They wrote: spoon sinks, apple sinks, pencil floats, lemon sinks. They dropped them in. The spoon sank. The pencil floated. But the apple and lemon bobbed on top. "We were wrong," Zainab said, surprised. "Write that too," said Madhav.

qa.q: What items did Madhav and Zainab test?
qa.a: A spoon, an apple, a pencil and a lemon.

qa.q: What does Zainab's surprise suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Zainab really expected the apple and lemon to sink and was learning from the result.

qa.q: What went well in their rushed experiment?
qa.a: They wrote their guesses first and recorded the real results, even the wrong ones.

qa.q: How might their teacher see their results?
qa.a: The teacher might be pleased they noticed and recorded what actually happened.

grounding: It shows children making predictions, testing and noticing results under time pressure.

passage: On the terrace of their Shillong flat, Maria and Dolma set two ice cubes on plates, one in the sun and one in the shade. "Mine in the sun will melt first," Maria said. "No, the shade one," said Dolma. They sat down to watch. After ten minutes, the sunny ice was almost a puddle, while the shade one was still solid. Dolma frowned. "Why?" Maria touched the sunny plate. "It's warm. The sun heats it." They wrote down what happened in Maria's notebook.

qa.q: Where did Maria and Dolma set the two ice cubes?
qa.a: One in the sun and one in the shade on the terrace.

qa.q: What does Dolma's frown suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Dolma was surprised and puzzled that the guess was wrong.

qa.q: What could Maria and Dolma try next?
qa.a: They could test different materials under the ice or try at different times of day.

qa.q: Why might Dolma see the result differently from Maria?
qa.a: Dolma's own guess was wrong, so Dolma may feel a little let down but curious, which is why Dolma asks why before they write it down.

grounding: It shows children predicting, testing and noticing what actually happened with melting ice.

passage:
"Which will float, the steel spoon or the plastic spoon?" Ujjwal, nine, asked, holding a bucket of water.

His sister Parul guessed, "Both will sink."

"I think plastic floats," Ujjwal said. He wrote both guesses on a paper.

He dropped them in. The steel spoon sank. The plastic one floated.

"Now the apple," Parul said.

"It's heavy, it'll sink."

It bobbed on top.

Ujjwal stared. "I was wrong! So heavy things can float?"

"Write it down," Parul said. He wrote: "Apple: guess sink, real float."

qa.q: What did Ujjwal predict for the apple?
qa.a: He said, "It's heavy, it'll sink."

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when the apple floated?
qa.a: He was surprised and curious, staring and wondering whether heavy things can float.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal do that makes this a real experiment?
qa.a: He wrote his guesses down before testing, then recorded what actually happened, so he could compare.

qa.q: How might Parul feel when her guess about the plastic spoon was wrong?
qa.a: She might feel a little surprised, but she stays interested and suggests testing the apple next.

grounding: A dialogue shows a child predicting, testing and noting what actually happened in a floating experiment.

passage:
Last month in Aizawl, our science teacher asked us to grow bean seeds. Samir and I guessed that seeds in the dark cupboard wouldn't grow at all.

We planted two cups. One on the window, one in the cupboard. We checked every morning and wrote in a notebook.

Day four: both had sprouts. We were surprised. Day ten: the cupboard one was taller but yellow and floppy. The window one was short, green and strong.

I didn't expect that. Samir said maybe the dark one was stretching to find light. So our guess was wrong, but we found out something better. I'm Lalremsiami, and I'm going to test mint next.

qa.q: Where did they put the two cups?
qa.a: One cup was on the window and one was in the cupboard.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami feel when the dark seed grew?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was surprised and curious, because it did not match the guess, and found the result exciting.

qa.q: Which parts of their method were good science?
qa.a: They made a guess, tested it with two cups, recorded daily and accepted the result even though it proved them wrong.

qa.q: What would change if they had not checked every morning?
qa.a: They might have missed when the sprouts appeared and how the plants changed, so their findings would be less clear.

grounding: A child recalls making a prediction about seeds, testing it and noticing a surprising result.

passage:
Science note, Class 4. Teacher: Pema.
Today we did “sink or float.” Before each test, children wrote a guess.
Yusuf (nine) guessed the big wooden block would sink, “because it's heavy.” It floated. He stared at it. He guessed the small steel key would float, “because it's tiny.” It sank.
He said, “Wait. It's not about big or small.” He tried a plastic lid, then a coin, writing each result.
At the end he wrote: “My guesses were wrong but I learned something.”
Next step: we'll try the same objects in salty water next week.

qa.q: What did Yusuf guess about the wooden block?
qa.a: He guessed it would sink, because it's heavy.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when the wooden block floated?
qa.a: He was surprised and puzzled, staring at it.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do after his guesses were wrong?
qa.a: He tested more objects and wrote each result, changing his idea about size.

qa.q: How might the teacher feel reading Yusuf's final sentence?
qa.a: The teacher likely feels pleased that Yusuf learned from his wrong guesses 🙂

grounding: A teacher notes a nine-year-old making predictions, testing them and noticing the results.

passage:
Sunday
Tarun and I planted two bean seeds last week. One in a cup on the window, one in a cup inside the cupboard. My guess: the cupboard one would grow slower because no sun.
Today we checked. The cupboard one is TALLER! But it's yellow and floppy. The window one is short, green and strong.
Tarun said, “So you were wrong.”
I said, “Half wrong. It grew faster but it's weak.” I don't know why yet. I'm going to ask Ms Jyoti tomorrow.
I wrote everything in my science notebook with drawings. — Neelam

qa.q: Where did Neelam put the second seed?
qa.a: In a cup inside the cupboard.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when the cupboard plant was taller?
qa.a: Neelam was surprised and curious, wanting to know why.

qa.q: What should Neelam do next as a young scientist?
qa.a: Ask Ms Jyoti and maybe try the test again with more seeds to see if the result repeats.

qa.q: How might Tarun see the result compared with Neelam?
qa.a: Tarun sees it simply as Neelam being wrong, while Neelam sees a more interesting answer.

grounding: A ten-year-old forms a guess about seeds, tests it and notices unexpected results.

passage:
In the hot afternoon in their village near Bikaner, Parul, eleven, and her friend Ankita had two ice cubes from the shop fridge.
“Which will melt first,” said Parul, “in the clay pot or the steel glass?”
Ankita guessed steel. “Steel gets hot.” Parul guessed the same.
They put one cube in each and sat in the shade, checking every few minutes.
The steel one melted first. But the clay pot's outside was wet and cool when Parul touched it.
“Why is the pot sweating?” Ankita asked.
Parul took out her notebook. “Let's write it down and ask Sir tomorrow.”

qa.q: Where did they put the ice cubes?
qa.a: One in the clay pot and one in the steel glass.

qa.q: How did the girls feel when the pot's outside was wet?
qa.a: They felt curious and puzzled, wanting to know why the pot was sweating.

qa.q: What did Parul do that shows good scientific thinking?
qa.a: She wrote down what happened and planned to ask the teacher instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might their teacher react to their question the next day?
qa.a: The teacher may be pleased and use it to explain how clay pots keep things cool.

grounding: Two village girls guess, test and observe how ice melts in clay and steel.

passage:
In Kraków, Marek and his friend Tariq filled the kitchen sink with water.
"Predictions," said Marek, grabbing a pencil. "The apple will sink. It's heavy."
Tariq thought. "The key will float. It's small."
They dropped them in. The apple bobbed on top. The key dropped straight down.
Marek stared. "Wrong. Both of us."
"Write it down anyway," said Tariq. "What we guessed, and what happened."
Marek wrote. Then: "So small doesn't mean float. Let's try a coin and a cork."

qa.q: What happened to the key?
qa.a: The key dropped straight down.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling when he stared at the apple floating?
qa.a: Marek felt surprised and puzzled, because it didn't do what he had predicted.

qa.q: Which habits of a good scientist did Marek and Tariq show?
qa.a: They wrote down their guesses and what really happened, then planned new tests instead of ignoring the surprise.

qa.q: How does Tariq see being wrong?
qa.a: Tariq sees it as part of the experiment, worth writing down, not something to hide.

grounding: Two children in Poland test predictions about floating and sinking and record the results.

passage:
In the school science lab, Ritu and Keerthana each had an ice cube on a plate.
"Salt will make it melt faster," said Ritu.
"No, slower. Salt is dry," said Keerthana.
They sprinkled salt on one cube and left the other plain. They wrote their guesses on the board and watched the clock.
After ten minutes, the salted cube was a puddle with a small lump left. The plain one was still mostly there.
Keerthana crossed out her guess. "I was wrong."
"Why does salt do that?" Ritu asked.
They went to find the teacher together.

qa.q: How long did they watch before checking the cubes?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she crossed out her guess?
qa.a: Keerthana may have felt a little disappointed, but she was honest about being wrong.

qa.q: What could Ritu and Keerthana do next to learn more?
qa.a: They could try the test again, maybe with sugar too, and ask the teacher why salt speeds up melting.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel about her prediction being right?
qa.a: Ritu likely feels pleased, but more curious than proud, since she immediately asks why.

grounding: Two children test a prediction about salt and ice and accept what actually happens.

passage:
I'm Vaibhav, Arohi's neighbour. For two weeks she had two bean plants on her windowsill, one in the sun, one inside a cardboard box.
She told me, "I think the one in the box will grow faster, because it's warm."
Every day she measured both with a ruler and wrote in a notebook.
At the end, the plant in the box was tall and thin and pale yellow. The one in the sun was shorter but green and strong.
Arohi looked at them for a long time. Then she wrote something, crossed it out, and wrote again. I think she was changing her answer.

qa.q: How long did Arohi keep the two bean plants on her windowsill?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What might Arohi have been feeling when she looked at the plants for a long time?
qa.a: Arohi seemed surprised and thoughtful, working out why her prediction didn't match.

qa.q: What did Arohi do that a good scientist would?
qa.a: She measured both plants every day, wrote the results down, and changed her answer when the results were different from her guess.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see Arohi's experiment?
qa.a: Vaibhav watches her closely but can only guess what she thinks, like when she seems to change her answer.

grounding: A neighbour watches a child test a prediction about plants and revise her conclusion.

passage:
Monday: Leela, ten, guessed that ice would melt faster in the sun than in the shade. Her friend Karthik said the opposite.
Tuesday: They put two ice cubes on plates, one on the sunny window, one in the shade. They checked every five minutes and wrote the times in a notebook.
Wednesday: They tried again with bigger cubes to be sure. The sunny cube melted first both days. Karthik shrugged. "You were right." Leela said, "We tested it. That's better than being right."

qa.q: How often did they check the ice?
qa.a: Every five minutes.

qa.q: How did Karthik seem to feel when the result came?
qa.a: He seemed a little disappointed but accepting, shrugging.

qa.q: Why was testing twice a good idea?
qa.a: It checked that the result was not a one-time accident.

qa.q: How might Leela's teacher see this experiment?
qa.a: The teacher would likely feel impressed by the guess, test and notes.

grounding: Tracks children forming a guess, testing it, and noticing the result.

passage:
Harsha, you're curious about my garden? Let me tell you how it started, one summer when I was nine.
I, Rehana, a curious girl, guessed that plants grow faster with music. My brother laughed. So I planted two pots of beans. One on the window with the radio, one on the window without.
Every day I measured with a ruler and wrote it down.
After two weeks, they were the same height. I was so disappointed.
My father said, "You found something out. That's science."
So, Harsha, guess. Test. And don't be sad if you were wrong.

qa.q: What did Rehana plant?
qa.a: Two pots of beans.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when both plants were the same height?
qa.a: Rehana felt disappointed.

qa.q: What was the lesson inside Rehana's story?
qa.a: Her father's point that finding out, even if the guess was wrong, is science.

qa.q: How might Rehana's brother have felt after the result?
qa.a: The brother may have felt smug but also curious about Rehana's careful test.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood experiment, testing a guess and accepting the result.

passage:
During the Diwali holidays, Leela, eleven, wanted to test which diya burned longest: one with ghee or one with oil. Her cousin Ganga said oil.
Then the wind blew out both diyas halfway through. Leela almost gave up.
Instead she moved the test indoors, relit them at the same time, and checked the clock every ten minutes.
The ghee diya lasted longer. Ganga frowned. "Maybe the wick was different."
Leela thought. "Good point. Tomorrow we use the same wick."

qa.q: What blew out both diyas?
qa.a: The wind.

qa.q: How did Leela feel when the diyas blew out?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and nearly gave up.

qa.q: What made Leela's test fair?
qa.a: She moved it indoors, relit both together, checked the clock, and planned to use the same wick.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel when Leela takes her point seriously?
qa.a: Ganga likely feels respected and interested.

grounding: Shows a child running a fair experiment despite complications.

passage:
During the Sankranti holidays it was cold enough that Pooja's breath made clouds. She had a question: does salt make ice melt faster?
"I think salt will make it slower," she told her cousin Jyoti, "because salt is dry."
They took two ice cubes from the freezer and put them on two steel plates. Pooja sprinkled salt on one. Jyoti timed them on the kitchen clock.
After ten minutes, the salted cube had a deep dip in it and a puddle around it. The plain cube still looked almost whole.
"I was wrong!" Pooja said, surprised. She wrote in her notebook: Guess, slower. Happened, faster.
"Why?" asked Jyoti.
"Don't know yet. Let's try sugar next."

qa.q: What did Pooja guess would happen with the salt?
qa.a: She guessed salt would make it slower, because salt is dry.

qa.q: How did Pooja feel when the salted ice melted faster?
qa.a: She felt surprised, but interested rather than upset, and happily wrote down what really happened.

qa.q: What could Pooja do to make the next test even fairer?
qa.a: She could keep the cubes the same size, use the same plates and time them together, changing only one thing, like salt or sugar.

qa.q: How might Jyoti see the experiment, as the one keeping time?
qa.a: Jyoti seems curious and involved, and by asking "Why?" she pushes Pooja to keep testing instead of stopping at one result.

grounding: Shows a child making a prediction, testing it and noticing what actually happened.
